subject: Technical deep dive — latency/throughput SLOs and deployment topology (recap)
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
To: Alex Johnson <alex.johnson@acme.com>
Cc: Dylan Brooks <dylan_brooks@redwood.com>, Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.com>

Subject: Technical deep dive — latency/throughput SLOs and deployment topology (recap)

Hi Alex / Acme SRE team,

Thanks again for taking the deep-dive with us today — appreciate the time. Below is a concise recap of the pain, goals, technical constraints you shared, and the immediate next steps we discussed. Please flag anything I missed.

1) Pain / motivation
- Gen-LLM features are adding variable latency to your search and client-facing assistants; worst-case spikes cause degraded UX during peak traffic.
- Current infra team struggles with unpredictable token costs and cold-start variability.

2) Goals / SLOs discussed
- Latency target: p95 end-to-end inference latency (in-region) <= 200 ms for typical prompt sizes (~300–500 tokens).
- Inference throughput: steady-state 120 QPS with bursts to 350 QPS for short windows (~5–10 min).
- Availability: 99.95% during business hours (US PST) with automatic fallback to a lower-cost model when capacity constrained.

3) Model & workload requirements
- Primary model: Llama-70B-class (quantized) with 8k context — customer expects comparable quality to current Llama-70B finetuned checkpoints.
- Many requests are short (2–50 tokens) but some long-context sessions (several hundred tokens) exist; KV cache reuse important.
- Sensitive PII: must run in your VPC/private deployment; no customer data to hosted multi-tenant environment.

4) Proposed deployment topology (high-level)
- Redwood Private (VPC) deployment in us-west-2 connected to Acme VPC via AWS Transit Gateway (or VPN).
- Dedicated GPU pool (reserved capacity) sized for steady-state 120 QPS; autoscale policy configured to allow bursts to 350 QPS for 10 minutes.
- Canary rollout path: start with dedicated reserved min capacity + 2x burst nodes; route a % of traffic during business hours and ramp.
- Cache strategy: prefix KV caching + request-level caching for repeat prompts; reduces token compute by estimated ~30% on top queries.

5) Operational notes / risk items
- Cold-start/warmup: depending on instance type and model quantization, warmup can be ~20–60s for fully cold GPU pools (we recommend pre-warmed instances during business hours).
- Security/compliance: we can provide SOC2 artifacts and network diagrams — your security team requested evidence during call.
- Cost expectation: we'll follow up with a detailed cost projection (instance + token estimates) after you confirm traffic shape and retention windows.

Next steps
- Action (Marissa): share detailed SLO/traffic worksheet and initial architecture diagram (attached).
- Action (Acme): confirm peak QPS windows and retention policy for KV cache (how long you want to keep session context).
- Schedule: aim for a follow-up demo and draft mutual action plan next week.

Attachments: slo_requirements_v1.pdf, arch-diagram.png, mutual-action-plan.xlsx

If that aligns, I'll start the cost estimate and a draft MxP.

Thanks,

Marissa Cole
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Technical deep dive — latency/throughput SLOs and deployment topology (recap)

Hi Marissa,

Thanks for the clear recap — this captures the discussion well. A few clarifications from our side:

- The 120 QPS steady-state assumes business-hour traffic across two regions (primary us-west, secondary us-east). The 350 QPS bursts are very short (usually under 7 minutes) tied to marketing pushes.
- Security: our InfoSec insists on Private deployment (VPC) and also requested the SOC2 Type II report + network diagram. Would you send the SOC2 evidence and a redacted network diagram?
- Warmup: can you quantify how many pre-warmed GPUs we'd need to handle the 350 QPS bursts without degrading p95? If warmup is ~20–60s then bursts may see higher tail latency unless we maintain some warm capacity.

Also: can you confirm fallback behavior if dedicated capacity is exhausted? We prefer automatic routing to a lower-cost model (smaller quantized variant) rather than rejecting requests.

Appreciate it — looped in the SRE alias for visibility.

— Alex
Alex Johnson
Head of Platform Engineering, Acme Robotics
alex.johnson@acme.com

Alex — quick answers inline and next steps below.

- Regions: noted — we'll propose a multi-region deployment (active-passive) with primary capacity in us-west and warm standby in us-east.

- SOC2 + diagram: attaching a redacted network diagram (arch-diagram.png) and a link to our SOC2 evidence bundle. We'll share the SOC2 Type II under NDA; let me know the contact for your procurement team and I'll route it.

- Warm capacity & burst handling: recommended approach:
  * Maintain a baseline of warm GPUs sized for ~60% of steady QPS (so warm pool ~72 QPS equivalent).
  * Autoscale + burst pool to handle spikes up to 350 QPS; burst pool scaled via reserved burst capacity (pre-provisioned instances) — expected warmup to scale from baseline to full burst capacity ~30–45s on average with optimized images.
  * For ultra-critical low-latency paths, we recommend sticky routing to always use the warm pool + aggressive prefix caching.

- Fallback behavior: yes — Redwood can automatically route to a compatible lower-capacity model variant (e.g., quantized 13B/30B family) when dedicated capacity is exhausted. We configure model-variant fallback with a circuit-breaker policy so that quality degrades gracefully instead of failing requests.

Next tangible steps:
- I'll upload an initial cost estimate and a sizing worksheet by EOD Tue (Dec 8).
- Please share the procurement contact so I can push SOC2 artifacts.
- Proposed follow-up: technical demo + mutual action plan review on Thu, Dec 10 — 11:00 AM PST.

Link: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1aBcD_example_arch_diagrams

Thanks,
Marissa
